Posted December 12, 2000
(MarijuanaNews note: Newspapers in the UK seem particularly gullible whenever the prohibitionists roll out the " Latest Research. " Certainly they gave the recent NIDA monkeyshines unquestioning coverage.
See
How NIDA Made Monkeys of the Media. 4 Primates Are News; 4 Million People Are Not. Analysis by Richard Cowan
and
Institute of Medicine Report on Medical Marijuana Contradicts Assumptions for NIDA Monkeyshines. Special to MarijuanaNews

So it should not be surprising that the down-market London Evening Standard had a header reading " CANNABIS SENDING FERTILITY TO POT. " Their article by Geraint Smith, their " Science Correspondent " began, " Smoking cannabis may seriously jeopardise the fertility of both men and women by giving sperm a huge " hit " on their way to the egg, American scientists said today. " What crap.

However, one expects much better from the venerable Scientific American Magazine. Alas, they too parroted the party line. The fact that the text does not correspond to the headline is common in tabloids, but should be unacceptable in a scientific journal.

However, the " research " on which they are reporting is based on a premise that no one seems to have checked. Do marijuana smokers really a problem with fertility? There are so many people in the world who smoke marijuana, and some groups – like the Rastafarians – who are very heavy smokers, this problem would be obvious, if it were real. This is just one more example of research finding a " cause " for which there is no effect.)

See
Marijuana and " Heart Attack " Report Tells Us More About Media And Politicized Medicine Than About Marijuana. -- 2 Articles

December 12, 2000
From The Scientific American Website
http://www.sciam.com
By Kristin Leutwyler
http://www.sciam.com/news/121200/2.html

BIOLOGY
Marijuana Firmly Linked to Infertility
(MarijuanaNews note: After the mandatory marijuana pun in the first sentence, notice the number conditional statements.)

Scientists from the University of Buffalo have smoked out what may cause some cases of infertility: marijuana. Today at the annual meeting of the American Society for Cell Biology, Herbert Schuel and his colleagues describe a cellular signaling system that responds to THC--the active substance in marijuana--and that may regulate sperm functions necessary for normal egg fertilization. The signaling system may be activated by anandamide, a cannabinoid-like molecule which this study shows for the first time is found in human seminal plasma, mid-cycle oviductal fluid and follicular fluid.

" These findings suggest that defects in the cannabinoid receptor-signaling system could account for certain types of infertility, " Schuel says. " A better understanding of these mechanisms might lead to the development of novel drugs useful in reproductive medicine. For heavy marijuana users, the study results raise the possibility they are jeopardizing fertility by overloading this system. "

To be sure, the process by which sperm prepare to fertilize an egg in the female reproductive tract is still mysterious. They must first become " capacitated " before they can begin swimming vigorously towards an egg and secrete the enzymes necessary to penetrate the egg's protective coat, a process called the acrosome reaction. But Schuel's work shows that both AM-356--a synthetic version of natural anandamide--and THC affect this sequence of events in three distinct ways: first, although low amounts of AM-356 stimulate sperm to swim more vigorously, too much of it has the exact opposite effect. Both AM-356 and TCH inhibit structural changes over the acrosome. And AM-356 significantly impairs sperm from binding to an egg's protective coat.

" The increased load of cannabinoids in people who abuse marijuana could flood natural endocannabinoid-signal systems in reproductive organs and adversely impact fertility, " Schuel adds. " This possibility may explain observations made over the past 30 to 40 years that marijuana smoke drastically reduces sperm production in males. "
(MarijuanaNews note: This kind of reporting may explain observations made over the past 30 or 40 years that there has been a decline in respect for " science " and other institutions.

Just where is the data to support this statement? Schuel used this point as the premise for his research, and therefore it is used to explain what he may have found. However, the most that can be said about this is that if a couple finds that they are having trouble conceiving, and one of them is a heavy marijuana smoker, they may want to reduce the marijuana use and keep trying.

As for the editors of The Scientific American, I would suggest that they may want to consider increasing their marijuana use and look up the word " Scientific " and keep trying.)
